title: Human wayfinding behaviour and metrics in complex environments: a systematic literature review
authors: Hassan Iftikhar, Parth Shah & Yan Luximon, 2021
review_question: The review aimed to address how well knowledge about human wayfinding behavior and metrics in complex environments has been established, identify areas of additional research, and understand the interrelationship of present contributions within the domain. Specifically, it addressed: RQ1: What factors make the university campus a complex environment for wayfinding? RQ2: What wayfinding metrics have been used for complex environments? RQ3: What are the impacts of culture, signage and unfamiliar environment on wayfinding behaviour? RQ4: What experimental settings have been designed for wayfinding research?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Articles related to complex environment wayfinding behaviour, signage-people understanding, and wayfinding using VR-based simulations were included. Specifically, institutional wayfinding behaviour (university campus), university campus signages, signage design, and wayfinding in VE were included in stage 2. Stage 3 focused on articles examining wayfinding behaviour in real/virtual complex environments and signage information design in cross-cultural settings. Only English journal articles published between Jan 1990 and Jan 2019 were included. Articles before 1990 primarily focused on city spaces and pedestrian navigation and were excluded.

findings.antecedent: University campus environment (congested layout, high-rise buildings, diffused pathways, multi-storey buildings, diffused facilities, multi-cultural community, lack of discrete boundaries, complex layout planning, inefficient environmental cues, shared social spaces, heavy concentration of people, visual richness, complexity in gaining familiarity, lack of functional space hierarchies)
findings.consequent: Wayfinding problems (disorientation, stress, frustration, time wasted, reduced legibility)
findings.quote: The university campuses situated in metropolitan city centres have morphed into complex environments due to congested layout and high-rise buildings. The environmental legibility for wayfinding within these environments is a great matter of concern.

findings.antecedent: Wayfinding task performance criteria (time taken to complete task, distance travelled, number of errors, path followed)
findings.quote: Various studies have evaluated human wayfinding performance based on task performance criteria. These studies have measured the time taken to complete a task, the distance travelled to the destination and the number of errors made during the task.

findings.antecedent: Space syntax methodologies (convex spaces, isovist fields, axial lines)
findings.consequent: Analysis of spatial features and wayfinding in indoor environments (e.g., underground train stations)
findings.quote: The combination of methodologies used for wayfinding evaluation of interior spaces has been described as space syntax... and found it effective in analysing the space.

findings.consequent: Evaluation of impacts of spatial forms, decision point actions, and signage effectiveness on real-world wayfinding behaviours
findings.quote: the space syntax methodologies cannot evaluate the impacts of spatial forms, decision point actions and the effectiveness of signage on real-world wayfinding behaviours

findings.antecedent: Cultural differences (understandings of spatial cues, cognitive strategies, interpretation of spatial cues)
findings.consequent: Human wayfinding behaviour (decision-making strategies, comprehension of spatial cues)
findings.quote: Culture, an inherently diverse element, is important in defining human wayfinding behaviour, because of the different understandings of spatial cues across different cultures.

findings.antecedent: Wayfinding signage design (textual, symbolic, colours, pictograms, information volume, placement)
findings.quote: Several spatial factors affect wayfinding performance and behaviour, including information signage. Studies have investigated the role of wayfinding signage design in hospital settings.

findings.antecedent: Standardization and consistency of spatial cues (including signage)
findings.quote: A few studies have also suggested that standardization and consistency of spatial cues can play a significant role in enhancing spatial comprehension.

findings.consequent: Wayfinding performance (relaxed and flexible information deduction, confidence, optimized route strategies, better performance with familiar signage)
findings.quote: Environmental familiarity allowed users to deduce the gathered information in a relaxed and flexible way... people who are familiar with an environment rely more on the retrieval of information from memory, cognitive memory and previous mental mapping of the environment, rather than on the environmental information.

findings.antecedent: Real-world wayfinding experiments (diversion of attention, path association, reflections, crowd movements, weather conditions)
findings.quote: Wayfinding experiments in real-world environments for evaluating behaviours have been accompanied by many confounding factors... It is quite difficult to achieve full control over the variables in real-world wayfinding experiments.

findings.antecedent: Computer Virtual Environments (VE) (desktop VR, AR systems, fully immersive VE with HMDs)
findings.consequent: Control over confounding factors in wayfinding experiments
findings.quote: computer VE can be considered an effective alternative to real-world wayfinding environments due to better control over confounding factors.

findings.consequent: Study of different emergencies (fire, earthquake, other emergency scenarios) for wayfinding research
findings.quote: VE can be used to study different emergencies, as they are quite complicated to conceive, control and perform in a real-world environment.

synthesis_conclusions: University campuses in city centers are complex environments causing wayfinding issues due to layout, facilities, and multi-cultural communities, leading to time wasted, stress, and frustration.
Wayfinding problems are caused by individual and cultural differences, layout unfamiliarity, and ineffective environmental information.
Textual and symbolic wayfinding information requires further investigation into varied user perception and comprehension, with culturally consistent design potentially enhancing understanding.
Digital natives (early 20s age group) are familiar with mobile devices, suggesting modern wayfinding solutions are needed for complex environments.

Virtual environments (VR/AR) offer better control over confounding variables for wayfinding research and are effective for simulating real-world emergency situations, but the efficacy of digital wayfinding information and ascribed user behavior still needs investigation.
evidence_gaps: Further investigation into varied user perception and comprehension of textual and symbolic wayfinding information due to individual and cultural differences.

Exploration of wayfinding aids, human cognition, human perceptions, and preferences for mitigating wayfinding difficulties in complex urban environments with multiple high-rise structures and fused facilities.
Comprehensive exploration of the impacts and efficiency of digital wayfinding information for digital natives.
Investigation into the efficacy of digital wayfinding information and ascribed user behaviour in virtual environments, especially for real-world emergency situations.
limitations: The review focused on specific keywords and databases, potentially missing relevant articles.
The qualitative nature of the review means no quantitative synthesis (e.g., meta-analysis) was performed.
